prompts.prompt: Name something sold in stick form (like deodorant; things on a stick don’t count).
prompts.hint: The example rules out food on a stick, so think of products that are sticks by design — lip care, glue, butter, incense and the things in a makeup bag. Everyday drugstore items are the common picks; trade tools and niche cosmetics are where the rare answers hide.

prompts.prompt: Name a food made by mashing or puréeing (like guacamole)
prompts.hint: Start with the dips and spreads — avocado, chickpeas, potatoes — then push into baby food, sauces and side dishes. Anything deliberately smooth counts, and the classic party dips are the crowded end.

answers.answer: Mashed broad beans with mustard greens

prompts.prompt: Name a country with the letter D in its name
prompts.hint: D shows up in country names more often than people expect — scan Europe, Africa, Asia and the Middle East, plus a few island states. Don't stop at the first one or two; the less famous names carry the points.

prompts.prompt: Name a device made to blow air
prompts.hint: Walk around a house — cooling, drying, heating, inflating — and the list nearly writes itself. Fans of every size are the obvious picks; the rare answers are the specialised tools that only move air as a side job.

prompts.prompt: Name a mammal smaller than a house cat
prompts.hint: A house cat weighs roughly four to five kilos, so the bar is low but real. Rodents, shrews, bats and small mustelids all fit — and be careful with animals that only look tiny, because plenty of them outweigh a cat.

prompts.prompt: Name something that has a saddle (like a bicycle)
prompts.hint: The bicycle example points at anything ridden — horses and other animals, motorbikes, gym machines. The everyday rides are the common answers; the clever picks are the things nobody thinks of as being ridden.

analysis: Almost nothing on this dive asks for a fact you would have to study. Stick-form products, air-blowing devices and things with saddles are objects everyone has handled a hundred times without ever listing them, so the whole page works as a slow-observation test. The players who pause and inventory the ordinary beat the ones who blurt out the first item that comes to mind.

Two rounds quietly check precision. The mammal question sets a real weight bar — a lot of animals look tiny but outweigh a house cat, and those near-misses cost exactly as much as a blank. The ISP prompt is the opposite problem: nobody needs knowledge to name their own provider, but the pool is geographic, so an answer that is obvious in one country can be nearly unique in another.

The stick-form question is the day's trap in friendly clothing: the parenthetical bans food on a stick and leaves only products that are sticks by design — glue, butter, incense, lip balm. The mashing prompt anchors everyone to guacamole and hummus before its points spread wide, and the letter-D countries keep yielding the longer you scan, which makes them the best place to bank a late, uncommon answer.
